steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm married filing jointly in Boston MA. W-2 from Metro Consulting: $79,400. Additional income: $12,500 (web design, 3 clients), $920 from Chase savings, $195 from Charles Schwab. Home office: 100 sq ft exclusive; I pay $2,400/month for 690 sq ft. Deductions: $3,600 student loan interest (MOHELA, 2017–2019); $800 to Doctors Without Borders I have the receipt; $780 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — I can walk you through how to treat each item, whether you should itemize, what forms to file, and what records to keep. I’m not a CPA, so consider this general guidance and — if you want — I can run more exact tax estimates or draft a summary you can share with your tax preparer.

Quick summary (recommendation)
- For federal 2024: you will almost certainly take the standard deduction (Married Filing Jointly) rather than itemizing.
- Report the $12,500 web‑design income on Schedule C (self‑employment). That makes you responsible for self‑employment tax (Schedule SE), but you can deduct half of SE tax on Schedule 1.
- Home office: you qualify (100 sq ft exclusive use). The actual method (allocation of rent) will almost certainly give a larger deduction than the simplified $5/sq ft method. If you use actual, complete Form 8829 (Business Use of Your Home) and attach it to Schedule C.
- Student loan interest: you can deduct up to $2,500 as an adjustment to income (Schedule 1), subject to income phaseouts. Based on the income you shared, you should be able to take the full $2,500 (you paid $3,600, but the federal cap is $2,500).
- Charitable $800 and unreimbursed expenses: charitable is deductible only if you itemize (so won’t help if you take the standard deduction). Unreimbursed employee expenses are not deductible for most employees (suspended through 2025); if the $780 are business expenses for your web‑design work, include them on Schedule C instead.

Detailed treatment and calculations (illustrative)
1) Income to report
- W-2 (Metro Consulting): $79,400 — report on Form 1040 wages.
- Self‑employment (web design): $12,500 — report on Schedule C (gross receipts). You’ll subtract business expenses there to get net profit.
- Interest: $920 (Chase) + $195 (Schwab) = $1,115 — report as taxable interest on Form 1040. (Schedule B only required if interest > $1,500; not required here.)

2) Business (self‑employment) items
- Schedule C: report gross receipts ($12,500) and business expenses. Include supplies, software, client expenses, and any of the $780 if those are business expenses (not unreimbursed employee expenses).
- Home office: you stated exclusive 100 sq ft of a 690 sq ft home.
  - Business percentage = 100 / 690 = 14.49%.
  - Rent = $2,400/month → $28,800/year × 14.49% = $4,176 (home‑office portion of rent).
  - Simplified method would be $5 × 100 sq ft = $500.
  - Because $4,176 (actual allocation just of rent) >> $500, the actual method will almost certainly be better. Use Form 8829 to compute the allowable deduction (you can include other allowable home expenses such as utilities if applicable).
  - Note: home‑office deduction cannot exceed net profit from the business. If your business net is small, excess home‑office deduction may carry forward.
- Other: the deductible part of self‑employment tax (half of SE tax) is an above‑the‑line adjustment (Schedule 1).

Illustrative net and adjustments (approximate)
- Business gross: $12,500
- Less home‑office (actual allocation of rent): ≈ $4,176
- Less other business expenses (if the $780 are business expenses): $780
- Estimated net profit ≈ $7,544
- Self‑employment tax is ~15.3% on 92.35% of net profit:
  - SE tax ≈ $1,066 → half deductible ≈ $533 (Schedule 1 adjustment)
- Student loan interest: you paid $3,600 but the federal above‑the‑line limit is $2,500 — so you can deduct $2,500 on Schedule 1 (subject to income phaseout; based on your totals you should be under the phaseout).
- These adjustments lower your AGI before your standard/itemized deduction.

3) Itemize vs standard deduction
- 2024 standard deduction (Married Filing Jointly): $29,200.
- Your listed itemizable items: $800 charitable + state income taxes (withheld) up to $10,000 SALT cap + possibly other items you did not list. Even with state taxes included, it’s very likely your itemized total will be well below the $29,200 standard deduction, so take the standard deduction.
- Note: charitable $800 only helps if you itemize.

4) State (Massachusetts, resident)
- File MA Form 1 for Massachusetts resident returns (state tax is a flat rate; check current MA rate for tax year 2024).
- Massachusetts taxes interest and self‑employment income; MA has its own rules/adjustments (and different treatment of student loan interest). I recommend checking MA DOR guidance or asking your preparer about state treatment of the student loan interest and any state deductions/credits. (I can pull MA specifics if you want.)

5) Forms you’ll need (federal)
- Form 1040 (Married Filing Jointly)
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — for student loan interest deduction and half of SE tax (adjustments)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report the web‑design income and business expenses
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you use the actual home‑office method (likely)
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax) — to compute SE tax
- Possibly Schedule B only if interest > $1,500 (not in your case)
- Keep copies of W-2, 1099‑NEC (if any clients issued one) or records of payment from clients, 1099‑INT/1099‑DIV, and 1098‑E (student loan interest statement) or loan statements.

6) Documentation you should keep
- W‑2 from Metro Consulting
- Records of web‑design income (invoices, bank deposits; any 1099‑NEC)
- Receipts for the $780 expenses and notes showing whether they’re business related
- Home records: lease agreement, monthly rent payments, floor plan showing 100 sq ft office area, photos showing exclusive business use — keep these in case of audit
- MOHELA (or other) statements / Form 1098‑E showing student loan interest paid
- Charity receipt for $800 (acknowledgment from Doctors Without Borders)
- Brokerage 1099‑INT / bank 1099‑INT statements for interest income

7) Other practical items
- Estimated taxes: because you have self‑employment income, you may need to make quarterly estimated tax payments for federal/state if withholding won’t cover your income tax + SE tax. If web‑design work continues in 2024, plan estimated payments for 2024 (due quarterly).
- If the $780 are unreimbursed expenses related to your W‑2 job (not your business), they are nondeductible under current law (through 2025).
- If you expect similar patterns next year, track expenses carefully and keep clear documentation of home‑office use.

Next steps / questions for you
- Are the $780 unreimbursed expenses related to the web‑design work (self‑employment) or to your W‑2 employment? If they are business expenses for the web work, include them on Schedule C.
- Do you want me to run a tighter tax estimate (approximate federal tax owed/refund and MA tax) using these numbers?
- Would you like a one‑page summary you can send to your tax preparer with the calculations and a documentation checklist?

If you want, I can (1) prepare the one‑page summary for your tax preparer, or (2) run a more precise federal + MA tax estimate based on the assumptions above. Which would you prefer?
